categories: ["ปวดท้อง", "รู้สึกหนาวและทนความเย็นไม่ได้"]
synonyms: ["Cold pain in the lower abdomen pulling toward the groin or genitals"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin can stem from a variety of causes, including inguinal hernias, genitourinary conditions, digestive issues like irritable bowel syndrome, or musculoskeletal strain. Diagnosis often involves physical examination, imaging such as ultrasound or CT scans, and lab tests to rule out infection, inflammation, or structural abnormalities. The pain is typically classified by its location, duration, and associated symptoms, but the underlying mechanism is usually understood as tissue irritation, nerve entrapment, or organ dysfunction.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment depends on the identified cause. For hernias, surgical repair is common. Musculoskeletal or nerve-related pain may be managed with rest, physical therapy, or anti-inflammatory medications. Gastrointestinal causes might be addressed with dietary changes, antispasmodics, or acid reducers. In cases where no clear structural cause is found, pain management with analgesics and watchful waiting is often recommended.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees this pain as a manifestation of Cold invading the body's lower regions, where it constricts the channels and disrupts the smooth flow of Qi and Blood. The Liver channel, in particular, wraps around the genitals and traverses the lower abdomen, making it the primary pathway through which Cold can trigger sharp, pulling sensations that radiate into the groin or testicles. When Cold enters this channel, it causes the tissues to contract and the Qi to stagnate, producing the characteristic cramping pain that worsens with exposure to cold and eases with warmth.
However, Cold rarely acts alone. Over time, it can combine with Dampness - especially in humid climates or in people who consume a lot of cold, raw foods - creating a heavy, dragging ache that feels like a cold weight in the lower belly. The tongue becomes puffy with a thick greasy coat, and the pulse feels slow and soggy. This pattern, Cold-Dampness in the Lower Burner, requires not just warming but also drying and transforming the excess moisture that is bogging down the Qi.
In other cases, persistent Cold penetrates deeper and congeals the Blood itself, much like ice forming in the vessels. This leads to a fixed, stabbing pain that does not migrate and often worsens with pressure. The tongue may appear bluish-purple, and the pulse becomes tight and choppy. This Blood Stagnation caused by Cold demands warming and invigorating herbs that break up the stasis while dispelling the underlying chill. Recognizing which pattern dominates is the key to effective treatment.
tcm_diagnosis:
When someone describes a cold, pulling pain in the lower abdomen that radiates toward the groin, a TCM practitioner first explores the exact quality of the pain and what makes it better or worse. Because cold is the root driver, warmth almost always brings relief, but the specific sensation and accompanying clues help distinguish which cold pattern is at work.
If the pain is sharp, spasmodic, and travels along the groin crease or into the scrotum, flaring suddenly with cold exposure, the picture points to Stagnation of Cold in the Liver Channel. This is the classic Cold Hernia (寒疝, hán shàn) presentation. The tongue is usually pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse feels tight and wiry (弦紧, xián jǐn), like a tense guitar string.
When the pain feels heavy, dull, and is accompanied by a sensation of cold dampness in the lower belly along with bloating, Cold-Dampness in the Lower Burner is more likely. This pattern often appears in damp climates or after eating cold, raw foods. The tongue coating becomes thick and greasy white, and the pulse is deep and slow (沉迟, chén chí), reflecting the sluggish, boggy nature of dampness.
If the pain is fixed, stabbing, and feels like a knife in one spot - especially after a long history of cold exposure - the practitioner suspects Blood Stagnation in the Lower Burner caused by Cold. Here the cold has congealed the blood, creating a sharper, unchanging pain that does not move. The tongue may show a dark purple body or purple spots, and the pulse is often choppy (涩, sè), signalling obstructed flow.

patterns.pattern_name: Stagnation of Cold in the Liver Channel
patterns.symptoms: ["Cold pain pulling to testicles or groin", "Scrotal contraction (in men)", "Pain worsens with cold exposure", "Relief with warmth", "Cold pain at the crown of the head", "Cold limbs"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold or damp weather, Eating cold or raw foods, Prolonged standing or heavy lifting, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth to the lower belly, Warm ginger, fennel, or cinnamon tea, Resting in a warm, quiet room, Gentle abdominal massage
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver channel runs through the lower abdomen, groin, and genitals. When external Cold invades and lodges in this channel, it constricts the flow of Qi and Blood, creating a sharp, cramping pain that pulls from the lower belly into the groin or testicles. The cold nature of the blockage makes the pain distinctly worse with cold exposure and noticeably better with warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body with a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, wiry, and slow or tight.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold contracts and tightens the Liver channel, so warmth is the most direct antidote - it relaxes the constriction and restores the smooth flow of Qi and Blood. Cold foods, cold environments, and physical strain all add more Cold and stagnation to the channel, worsening the pain. Emotional stress can cause Qi to knot up, which combines with Cold to make the blockage even tighter.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower abdomen and groin warm with a heating pad or warm compress. Sip warm ginger tea and add cinnamon, fennel, or cloves to meals. Avoid iced drinks, raw salads, and cold smoothies. Gentle walking or stretching can help keep Qi moving without straining the area.

patterns.worse_with: Cold or damp weather, Eating cold or raw foods, Sitting on cold surfaces, Prolonged standing or heavy lifting
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth to the lower belly, Dry weather, Warm cooked meals, Gentle abdominal massage, Resting in a warm, quiet room
patterns.why_this_happens: Cold contracts and obstructs, while Dampness weighs down and blocks the flow of Qi. When these two pathogens settle in the lower abdomen, they create a deep, cold ache that feels heavy and dragging. The stagnant Qi and fluids press downward, often pulling toward the groin along the pelvic channels, especially in damp or cold weather.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: deep, slow, and soggy, especially in the rear (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and Dampness are Yin pathogens that contract and obstruct Qi. Warmth and dryness naturally disperse them, easing the heavy, dragging pain. Cold, damp environments and raw foods add more Cold and Dampness to the body, worsening the obstruction. Rest and gentle massage allow Qi to move without straining, while overexertion and prolonged standing increase the downward pressure of Dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews; avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods. Keep the lower abdomen and feet warm, especially in damp weather. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi flow and dries internal Dampness.

patterns.pattern_name: Blood Stagnation in the Lower Burner  caused by Cold
patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing lower abdominal pain that may radiate to the groin", "Pain worsens with cold and eases with warmth or a hot water bottle", "Dark, purplish menstrual blood with clots (in women)", "Cold sensation in the lower belly and cold hands and feet"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold or damp weather, Eating cold or raw foods, Prolonged sitting in a cold place, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth to the lower belly, Warm ginger, fennel, or cinnamon tea, Gentle abdominal massage, Resting in a warm, quiet room
patterns.why_this_happens: When Cold lingers in the lower burner, it freezes and congeals the Blood, much like water turning to ice. This creates a fixed, stabbing pain that can pull toward the groin because the stuck Blood blocks the free flow of Qi along the channels that pass through that area.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-purple or bluish-purple body, possible stasis spots, white slippery coat. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), tight (紧 jǐn), and choppy (涩 sè), reflecting interior Cold constriction and Blood Stasis.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold is the root cause here, congealing Blood like ice. Anything that warms the body-a hot compress, warm drinks, moxibustion-melts that Cold and helps Blood flow freely again, relieving the stabbing pain. Conversely, cold weather, raw foods, and a chilly environment add more Cold, thickening the stasis. Emotional stress stagnates Qi, which is needed to push Blood, so staying calm and relaxed prevents the blockage from worsening.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower abdomen and feet warm, especially in cold months. Eat warming, Blood-moving foods like ginger, cinnamon, lamb, black beans, and cooked dark leafy greens. Avoid icy drinks, raw salads, and dairy, which introduce internal Cold. Gentle daily movement such as walking or yoga helps keep Blood flowing, but avoid strenuous exercise in cold weather.

faqs.question: Does this mean I have a hernia?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. In TCM, “Cold Hernia” (寒疝) refers to a pattern of pain and constriction caused by Cold, not always a physical protrusion of tissue. However, a real inguinal hernia can produce similar symptoms. If you feel a bulge in the groin or scrotum, or if the pain is sudden and severe, seek a medical evaluation to rule out a structural hernia before or alongside TCM treatment.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with this type of pain?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can be very effective at moving Qi and Blood in the lower abdomen and warming the channels. Points like Guanyuan (REN-4) and Zusanli (ST-36) are often used with moxibustion - a gentle heat therapy - to directly expel Cold. Most patients feel a soothing warmth during treatment and may notice less pain within the first few sessions.

faqs.question: What should I eat if I have cold lower abdominal pain?
faqs.answer: Focus on warming, cooked foods. Think soups, stews, and teas made with ginger, cinnamon, fennel, or cardamom. Avoid raw salads, iced drinks, dairy, and cold fruits, as these introduce more Cold and Dampness into the body. Even a simple cup of hot ginger tea with meals can make a noticeable difference.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use herbs while trying to conceive or during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Some warming herbs are contraindicated in pregnancy because they strongly move Blood and Qi. Always inform your TCM practitioner if you are pregnant or trying to conceive. They will select safe, gentle alternatives and may rely more heavily on acupuncture and moxibustion to manage pain without risk.

faqs.question: How long will it take before I feel better?
faqs.answer: Many patients experience some relief within the first week of herbal treatment and acupuncture, especially if the pain is primarily from Cold invasion. Patterns involving Dampness or Blood Stasis tend to improve more gradually over 3 to 6 weeks. Full resolution and prevention of recurrence often require 2 to 3 months of consistent care and lifestyle adjustments.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with painkillers or other medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. TCM herbs and acupuncture can complement conventional pain management. However, some warming and Blood-moving herbs may interact with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs. Always share your full medication list with your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor to coordinate care safely.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic pelvic pain: A systematic review
research.description: This systematic review evaluated acupuncture for chronic pelvic pain conditions, many of which include lower abdominal pain with radiation. It concluded that acupuncture provides moderate relief and is a safe adjunct. The review noted that warm needling techniques, which correspond to treating cold patterns, showed particularly good results in sub-analyses.
research.periodical: Lee EJ, Frazier SK. Acupuncture for chronic pelvic pain: A systematic review. Pain Management Nursing. 2011 Sep;12(3):153-60.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for functional abdominal pain syndrome: From clinical findings to basic understandings
research.description: This review outlined the TCM pathogenesis of functional abdominal pain as commonly involving Spleen Yang vacuity and Cold congealing. It highlighted the use of warming formulas like Liang Fu Wan and their pharmacological basis for relieving cold-type abdominal pain and visceral hypersensitivity.
research.periodical: Li H, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for functional abdominal pain syndrome: From clinical findings to basic understandings. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2016;2016:1-15.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of traditional Chinese medicine for chronic pelvic pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis examined TCM treatments for chronic pelvic pain and found that warming and blood-moving herbal formulas combined with acupuncture significantly outperformed conventional analgesics for pain relief. Subgroup analysis supported the advantage in patients presenting with cold-type pain symptoms.
research.periodical: Huang Y, et al. Efficacy and safety of traditional Chinese medicine for chronic pelvic pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Pain Research. 2021;14:2259-2274.
